documents.title: Sec. 5-95. - Architectural approach.
documents.text:
(a)
Drawing from the rich heritage of Colorado's land and the intrinsic character of its
architecture, the built environment of Sterling Ranch will reflect all that is inherently
Colorado.
Architectural Environment of Villages
(b)
Architecturally, Sterling Ranch will feature vernaculars born in Colorado that encapsulate
its spirit. Though rooted in the past, the specified styles will seek to fully capture
an aesthetic that is authentic to Colorado through the implementation of materials,
massing, and forms consistent with present design.
(c)
Additionally, Modern Colorado vernaculars will also be allowed as it is outlined.
The Modern Colorado styles will bridge the gap between the historic and contemporary,
reflecting Colorado's distinct architectural character today.
(d)
Each village of Sterling Ranch will incorporate two primary traditional Colorado architectural
styles with the Modern Colorado style interspersed throughout. Selected styles for
each individual village will distinguish one village's character from another. Additional
design styles and details will be found in village-specific guidelines of Sterling
Ranch.
Architectural Design Styles
(e)
The continuity of the architecture, in conjunction with its location, will establish
Sterling Ranch as a well-defined, unique sense of place, providing a cohesive framework
for the community's overall aesthetic. Its Colorado-inspired vernaculars will create
a sense of timelessness and establish Sterling Ranch as a community to emulate.
(Rules of 8-26-2020(9), § 4.1)

documents.title: Sec. 5-96. - Lot programming.
documents.text:
Throughout Sterling Ranch, homes shall be sited with care to ensure a diverse street
scene. In order to achieve variety, the following requirements shall be implemented:
Architectural Diversity
(1)
Homes with the same floor plan shall not be adjacent to each other, or directly across
the street.
(2)
Every third home shall have a different garage configuration (lot size permitting).
Major roof silhouettes shall be varied every third house. A sense of entry is required
of all home designs with visible front doors whenever possible.
(3)
Identical floor plans, elevations, and colors may not alternate to achieve maximum
variety on each street at the discretion of the Design Review Committee.
(4)
The Design Review Committee reserves discretion to preserve a diverse and varied streetscape
through master plan and plot plan reviews.
These overall requirements will reinforce diversity in design throughout the development
of Sterling Ranch.
(Rules of 8-26-2020(9), § 4.2(intro. ¶))

documents.title: Sec. 5-97. - Icon lots.
documents.text:
(a)
Icon lots are reserved for prominently located homes that feature single-story edges,
corner garages, and will include enhanced architecture on all four sides. Materials
shall wrap as necessary to inside corners. Plane breaks may also be required depending
on architectural style, materials, and articulation. Ultimately, these highly visible
homes will require four-sided architecture to add to the overall appeal and character
of the community. Icon lots shall also require additional landscaping.
(b)
The Design Review Committee (DRC) reserves the right to re-evaluate icon and enhanced
lots at Plot Plan Submittals; additional information and maps will be issued for future
filings not already in specific village guidelines.
(Rules of 8-26-2020(9), § 4.2(A))

documents.title: Sec. 5-98. - Enhanced lots.
documents.text:
(a)
Enhanced lots require that design elements featured on the front elevation of homes
be carried to exposed side and/or rear elevations. Overall, the goal is to create
well-articulated elevations that reinforce the architectural character on exposed
side or rear elevations. Enhanced lots shall also require additional landscaping.
Refer to specific village landscape and lot maps for required enhancements.
(b)
The Design Review Committee (DRC) reserves the right to re-evaluate icon and enhanced
lots at Plot Plan Submittals; additional information and maps will be issued for future
filings not already in specific village guidelines.
(Rules of 8-26-2020(9), § 4.2(B))

documents.title: Sec. 5-99. - Garage configurations.
documents.text:
(a)
A variety of garage configurations will be required for Sterling Ranch to create and
maintain a diverse street scene throughout the community.
Garage Configuration Varieties
(b)
No more than 33 percent of a builder series shall have the garage-forward configuration.
No more than 50 percent of front footage can be garage. The following configurations
shall comprise all allowable garage formats for the entire development: Refer to section 5-212 .
(Rules of 8-26-2020(9), § 4.3)

documents.title: Sec. 5-121. - General scope and design criteria.
path: Sec. 5-121. - General scope and design criteria.
documents.text:
The standards of this division are guiding principles for the residential villages
of Sterling Ranch. Each principle provides a framework for the community, and promotes
high quality, unique representations of the vision behind this uncommon, master-planned
development. Criteria may vary per village.
Community Framework of Village Developments
(Rules of 8-26-2020(9), § 5.1(intro. ¶))

documents.title: Sec. 5-122. - Massing and scale.
documents.text:
(a)
The massing shall reflect the architectural styles specified.
Massing
(b)
No more than 33 percent of any home's elevation shall have three stories stacked on
an uninterrupted plane. May vary per village.
(c)
The use of single-story elements is encouraged to produce variation at the street
level.
(Rules of 8-26-2020(9), § 5.1(A))

documents.title: Sec. 5-123. - Roof forms.
documents.text:
(a)
Roof forms shall reflect the style of the home.
Roof Form
(b)
Large, out-of-scale roof areas are not encouraged.
(c)
A variety of roof silhouettes are required.
(d)
Every third home in a row shall have a different primary roof form. May vary per village.
Refer to section 5-214 .
(Rules of 8-26-2020(9), § 5.1(B))

documents.title: Sec. 5-124. - Doors and windows.
documents.text:
(a)
Doors and windows shall be implemented in an organized pattern.
Doors and Windows
(b)
A strong hierarchy in the layout of doors and windows is required on all elevations.
(c)
Recessed windows and other such detailing on flat facades are desired to provide shade,
shadow, and texture.
(d)
The window style shall be consistent on all four sides.
(e)
The window style shall correspond to the aesthetic of the home.
(f)
The size and scale of the windows shall enhance the home's overall feel.
(Rules of 8-26-2020(9), § 5.1(C))

documents.title: Sec. 5-125. - Masonry.
documents.text:
(a)
Sixty percent of the homes in a builder series shall include some masonry; this includes,
but is not limited to, stone, brick, stucco, and concrete block veneers.
Masonry
(b)
Masonry shall have logical termination points; whether the material wraps from one
side to another, or is limited to a single element.
(c)
Stone must end at inside corners, and wrap two feet from any facade.
(Rules of 8-26-2020(9), § 5.1(D))

documents.title: Sec. 5-126. - Decks and porches.
documents.text:
(a)
Rear decks and balconies cannot project outwards more than they are recessed inwards.
Decks and Porches
(b)
No more than 33 percent of the houses may have three stories stacked to further ensure
a varied rear elevation scene. To break from the three-story stacking norm, single-story
elements will be implemented to vary detached, walkout elevation compositions. May
vary per village.
(c)
Front porches are encouraged throughout the community, if applicable to the elevation
style, as they promote an inviting streetscape.
(Rules of 8-26-2020(9), § 5.1(E))

documents.title: Sec. 5-127. - Articulation.
documents.text:
(a)
A rear offset of at least three feet, zero inches shall be required to avoid flat,
rear elevation compositions. For smaller lots, this criteria may be reduced.
Elevation Articulation
(b)
Same or like floorplans and elevations shall not be repeated side by side on alternating
lots or across the street. The overall street scene must employ variation and diversity
in its designs to add visual interest to the community.
(Rules of 8-26-2020(9), § 5.1(F))

documents.title: Sec. 5-128. - Garage configurations.
documents.text:
(a)
Two-car garage forward.
(1)
The two-car garage forward format shall be designed to reduce the appearance of the
garage.
(2)
All plans with this garage configuration shall include a porch or architectural entry
treatment to further diminish the appearance of the garage.
(b)
Three-car garage forward.
(1)
The three-car garage forward format shall be designed to diminish the appearance of
the garage's width.
(2)
Architecture shall mitigate the appearance of the garage.
(3)
This format is allowable on only 25 percent of the homes; and no more than two homes
with this configuration shall appear side by side.
(4)
A minimum offset of two feet, zero inches shall be required between the two- and one-car
garages.
(5)
At three-car garages, the garage doors shall not take up more than 50 percent of the
home.
(6)
Another 25 percent of three-car garage front configuration is allowed if the forward-most
garage is recessed ten feet from the forward-most living space for a total of 50 percent
for lot sizes and product that comply with Section 5-147 .
(c)
Side load garage.
(1)
The side load garage may be implemented as lot widths allow.
(2)
Side load garages are encouraged at corner lots.
(3)
Street-facing garage facades may require additional enhancements.
(d)
Single family—alley loaded.
(1)
Single family—alley loaded may be in either a detached or attached format.
(2)
Single family—alley loaded are preferred in site locations that edge areas allocated
for mixed use, or that face parks and main streets.
(e)
Recessed garage.
(1)
Garage shall be recessed a minimum of five feet from porch or forward-most living
area.
(2)
All plans with this garage configuration shall include a porch or architectural entry
treatment to further diminish appearance of garage.
(f)
Deep recessed garage.
(1)
Garages in deep recessed format are set toward the rear of the lot to diminish the
garage's appearance.
(2)
Rear-lot recessed garages must be in the rear one-third of the lot and may be detached.
(g)
Turn-in garage.
(1)
A turn-in garage creates visual diversity as it breaks monotony of front-facing garages
to the street.
(2)
A turn-in garage may be a two-car or three-car turn-in.
(3)
A turn-in garage minimizes the appearance of the garage, while maximizing functionality.
(4)
A turn-in garage offers flexibility in appearance, articulation, and plan format.
(5)
A two-foot, zero-inch offset is required on three-car garages.
(6)
Street-facing garage facades may require additional enhancements.
(h)
One-two split garage.
(1)
One-car straight-in and two-car turn-in garages.
(2)

documents.title: Sec. 5-128. - Garage configurations.
documents.text:
Entry to the home is accessed between the one-car and two-car garages.
(3)
At one-two split garages, a sense of entry must be maintained, if direct visibility
of the front door is not possible.
(4)
Street-facing garage facades may require additional enhancements.
(i)
Two-one split garage.
(1)
Two-car straight-in garage with a one-car turn-in garage.
(2)
Entry to the home is accessed between the two garages.
(3)
At two-one split garages, a sense of entry must be maintained, if direct visibility
of the front door is not possible.
(4)
Street-facing garage facades may require additional enhancements.
(j)
Two-one split garage, side entry.
(1)
Two-car straight-in garage with a one-car turn-in garage.
(2)
Entry to the home is accessed on the side of the house.
(3)
At two-one split garages with side entries, a sense of entry must be maintained, if
direct visibility of the front door is not possible.
(4)
Street-facing garage facades may require additional enhancements.
(k)
Corner lot garage.
(1)
On corner lots, the garage may be repositioned from its original format to take access
from the adjacent side street.
(2)
A corner lot garage offers further opportunities for lot and elevation enhancements.
(3)
This is a preferred solution for icon lots when possible.
(l)
Two-one split garage forward.
(1)
Two-car straight-in garage with a one-car straight-in garage.
(2)
A two-one split garage forward design allows for front door visibility and unique
floor plan opportunities.
(3)
This is not preferred solution and other two-one split garage solutions are encouraged.
(m)
Two-one motor court split.
(1)
Two-car straight-in garage with a one-car turn-in garage accessed through a porte-cochere
and off a shared motor court.
(2)
A two-one motor court split design allows direct visibility to the front door and
creates a strong presence to the street.
(3)
Street-facing garage facades may require additional enhancements.
(n)
Attached, alley-loaded.
(1)
Two-car alley-loaded, attached garage.
(2)
An attached, alley-loaded garage presents a strong street edge for higher density,
or highly visible areas, while allowing for rear access.
(o)
Duplex, paired garage.
(1)
A duplex, paired garage format shall be designed to reduce the appearance of the garage
and to promote privacy at entries.
(2)
In 50 percent of the duplexes, both garages may face the street; however, in no case
may garages exist in the same place without recess (i.e., two, two-car garages directly
next to one another).
(p)
Four-pac cluster.
(1)
2-story plans oriented in a four-pac cluster.
(2)

documents.title: Sec. 5-128. - Garage configurations.
documents.text:
A combination of front units featuring two-car front-loaded garages and rear units
featuring two-car side-loaded garages, or four-sided loaded garages.
(3)
Front units take pedestrian and vehicle access directly off a main street while rear
units take access off a shared motor court.
(4)
Individual driveways provide parking for each unit.
(Rules of 8-26-2020(9), § 9.1)

documents.title: Sec. 5-129. - Typical lot setbacks.
documents.text:
(a)
Generally.
(1)
All setbacks listed are minimums.
(2)
Corner lots shall have a seven-foot minimum secondary frontage setback to the building.
Ten feet is preferred.
(3)
Corner lots have a six-foot utility easement.
(4)
Decks and patios 30 inches or less above grade may encroach into the rear setback
a maximum of five feet. Open or enclosed decks on the main level of a walkout condition
may encroach into the rear setback provided they are no closer than 15 feet to the
rear property line.
(5)
Balconies and bay windows may encroach up to one-quarter of the depth of the building
front setback except that balconies on porch roofs may encroach as does the porch.
(6)
Relief from front setbacks shall be permitted to accommodate front yard slopes over
15 percent.
(7)
Fences and easements shall be permitted within setbacks.
(8)
All encroachments and setbacks must meet Douglas County building permit requirements.
(9)
Window wells, a cornice, canopy, eave, fireplace, wing wall or similar architectural
feature may extend up to three feet into a required setback.

documents.title: Sec. 5-130. - Roof-type illustrations and examples.
documents.text:
To establish a diverse and pleasing street experience throughout the entire Sterling
Ranch Community, the Sterling Ranch Community Authority Board (CAB) enforces a Roof
Form Variety Rule, which requires that every third home in a row implement a different
primary roof form. Additionally, the Design Review Committee requires that adjacent
homes, or homes directly across the street, employ a different primary roof form.
Out of this aim, the following roof type illustrations and examples have been created
to illustrate how roof types are defined and evaluated by the DRC. The Sterling Ranch
DRC and CAB reserve the right to deny the approval and construction of any design
that fails to meet the aforementioned requirements.

documents.title: Sec. 5-147. - Intent.
documents.text:
(a)
These landscape design standards are intended to highlight the vital landscape principles
that enhance and complement the community character for all of Sterling Ranch. Water
Demand Management Initiatives included in this Code contain more detailed landscape
and irrigation specifications, a list of preapproved plant species, professional registration
requirements, builder-provided homeowner education requirements, information on submittal,
inspection, and certification processes, as well as detailed information on water
budgets for individual lots.
(b)
An essential component of natural resource stewardship and responsible water management
is specifying a significant portion of plant material that is native, naturalized,
or adapted to the semi-arid high plains prairie ecosystem in which Sterling Ranch
is located. By incorporating the native or naturalized plantings of this geographic
region in a way that meets the aesthetic character of the community, Sterling Ranch
will be a showcase of water demand management and a successful blending of nature
and development.
(Rules of 8-26-2020(9), § 6.1)

documents.title: Sec. 5-148. - Soils.
documents.text:
Soil preparation is essential to the success of new landscaping. Planting and turf
beds must be treated and prepped before installing plant material or an irrigation
system. The soil in Sterling Ranch has very limited organic material and must be amended
accordingly.
(1)
A minimum of four cubic yards of soil amendment per 1,000 square feet of landscaped
area must be applied over the existing ground surface and tilled to a depth of at
least six inches. The soil amendment itself must be a combination of ground aged manure
and organic compost.
(2)
The graded site shall be free of rock, debris, and dirt clods over three-quarter inch
in diameter. Existing topsoil should be salvaged and stockpiled for use as soil amendments
or topsoil.
(Rules of 8-26-2020(9), § 6.2)

documents.title: Sec. 5-149. - Groundcover.
documents.text:
(a)
Mulch is required to help plant material retain moisture, reduce weeds and prevent
soil erosion. Fibrous wood mulch is the preferred mulch in perennial planting beds;
however, naturally colored angular rock mulch, or pea gravel mixed with larger squeegee-sized
rocks are encouraged in shrub beds. Rounded river cobble may be used where drainage
conditions preclude the use of wood mulch.
(b)
Non-dyed, shredded cedar is the preferred type of wood mulch.
(c)
Naturally colored rock mulch with commercial grade weed barrier fabric is preferred
in shrub beds. Rounded river cobble (two inches to four inches diameter) is also acceptable,
but is preferred in limited applications such as drainage swales. Non-earthen-tone
mulch materials, such as white or black granite rock, are to be used as accents in
the yard only and require DRC approval.
(d)
Wood mulch should cover the planting beds to a minimum depth of three inches.
(e)
Continuous commercial grade weed barrier fabric should be installed at planting installation
where appropriate.
(f)
A continuous edger should be installed between the plant bed and lawn.
(g)
All exposed soil shall be covered with mulch at a rate of one cubic yard per 80 square
feet, or a depth of four inches, and as appropriate to each species. Inorganic mulches
such as rock, pebbles, and gravel shall have a minimum depth of two inches; rock mulch
of one to 1½ inches in diameter is preferred.
(Rules of 8-26-2020(9), § 6.3)

documents.title: Sec. 5-150. - Irrigation.
documents.text:
(a)
Water demand management initiatives have been developed for Sterling Ranch to achieve
two of its major hallmarks: the commitment to water management and stewardship of
natural resources. As a part of these Water Demand Management Initiatives, exterior
water budgets have been pre-determined for varying lot sizes. Refer to Section 9-76 .
(b)
There is flexibility in using these water budgets to meet individual landscaping styles.
For example, an area that is planted entirely with shrubs and trees, and irrigated
with a drip system, will have a lower water demand than the same area planted entirely
with turf and irrigated with a spray system. Following the water budget approach utilized
by Sterling Ranch, the size of the irrigated area can be enlarged by increasing the
number of low water use plantings and decreasing the number of high water use areas.
(1)
The water budget approach of Sterling Ranch signifies that each lot is given a specific
amount of water according to its lot size.
(2)
Planting and irrigation plans must be submitted to and approved by the Sterling Ranch
Design Review Committee. Planting and irrigation designs should be coordinated to
ensure water budgets are not exceeded. Please refer to the Sterling Ranch water demand
management initiatives for more information on water budget, irrigation specifications,
and submittal requirements, which are adopted by the Community Authority Board (CAB).
(3)
Builders are required to design and install landscaping and irrigation systems in
the front yard.
(4)
Builders are not required to design and install landscaping and irrigation systems
in the backyard. However, builders must make available to home buyers as an optional
upgrade landscape and irrigation plans for each model home type, as well as installation
services.
(5)
When designing the landscape, it is important to note that a maximum of 30 percent
of the total water budget may be utilized for the front yard and right-of-way to ensure
an adequate budget of water remains for the backyard.
(6)
By installing efficient irrigation systems and water-smart plantings suited for the
semi-arid climate in Sterling Ranch, builders and homeowners have the opportunity
to expand their landscaped area and improve the functionality of their outdoor living
space.
(7)
Overhead irrigation is not allowed in areas less than eight feet in width, or on slopes
greater than 4:1. Drip or other subsurface irrigation is required in these narrow
and steep areas.
(8)
In general, only turf grass and native species may have overhead irrigation. Trees,

documents.title: Sec. 5-150. - Irrigation.
documents.text:
shrubs, perennials, and groundcovers shall be irrigated with a form of drip technology.
(c)
Homeowner education. Builders shall provide homeowner education regarding installed
outdoor water demand management measures.
(1)
Builders shall provide a written operating and maintenance manual for all water-using
equipment or controls installed.
(2)
Builders are required to provide homeowners the Sterling Ranch water demand management
initiatives and clearly identify the water budget remaining for any homeowner-installed
backyards.
(3)
Builders shall provide two watering schedules for all installed irrigation systems,
and post the schedules at the irrigation system controller. One schedule shall be
designed for the establishment period, and the second schedule shall be designed for
the permanent landscape. Both schedules shall vary by season.
(4)
Builders shall provide a schematic of any installed irrigation system along with an
itemized list of irrigation components, copies of irrigation schedules, and information
on reprogramming the controller.
(Rules of 8-26-2020(9), § 6.4)

documents.title: Sec. 5-151. - Required lot landscape.
documents.text:
(a)
Artificial turf will be evaluated on an individual basis for front yards.
(b)
The front yard shall consist of a combination of trees, sodded turf, and shrubs. Perennial
and groundcover beds are not required, but are strongly encouraged to provide variety
and personalization to the home. Annual plantings may also be part of the overall
design.
(c)
Front yard design and installation shall include trees and plants as specified below:
(1)
One deciduous tree (minimum two-inch caliper).
(2)
One evergreen tree (minimum six feet in height) or one ornamental tree (minimum 1½-inch
caliper).
(3)
80 percent live coverage.
(4)
A minimum of three types of perennials, ornamental grasses, or groundcovers.
(5)
A minimum of three types of shrubs.
(6)
Front yard is not required to include sodded turf, but any turf installed must be
sodded.
(7)
A variance may be granted to allow for one required front yard tree for smaller lot
product when irrigated area is restrictive.
Front Yard Landscaping
(d)
No wood planter boxes are permitted in the front yard.
(e)
Front yard landscape must be completed by the builder no later than 30 days after
closing. If the rear yard landscape is installed by the builder as an optional upgrade,
it must be completed within 120 days following closing. A winter deferral period is
granted for closings from November 1 to April 30.
(f)
The builder shall install similar rock and/or wood mulch in front yards between adjacent
houses to unify the streetscape.
(g)
Plantings on corner lots must meet Douglas County safety requirements for Sight Visibility
Triangles.
(h)
Side yard visible from the street shall include:
(1)
A minimum of three types of perennials, ornamental grasses, and/or groundcovers.
(2)
A minimum of three types of shrubs.
(3)
60 percent live coverage.
(i)
Side yard on corner lots shall include:
(1)
A minimum of three types of perennials, ornamental grasses, and/or groundcovers.
(2)
A minimum of three types of shrubs.
(j)
Backyard landscaping also must include two trees as specified below:
(1)
One deciduous tree (minimum 1½-inch caliper).
(2)
One evergreen tree (minimum six to eight feet in height).
Typical Rear Yard Landscaping
(k)
Artificial turf will be evaluated on an individual basis for backyards.
(l)
The backyard must contain a minimum of 30 percent live plant material (groundcovers,
turf, grasses, perennials, shrubs, trees, etc.). Tree canopies alone will not be counted
towards satisfying any live coverage requirements.
(m)
An automatic, underground irrigation system is required for all parts of the yard
that require water.
(n)

documents.title: Sec. 5-151. - Required lot landscape.
documents.text:
Landscape and irrigation plans for each residence at Sterling Ranch must be submitted
for review and approval by the Design Review Committee (DRC).
(o)
In instances where the size of the front yard or building footprint precludes one
deciduous and one evergreen tree from being planted, trees may be substituted with
additional shrubs or grasses at a rate of ten shrubs/grasses per tree. Narrow upright
evergreen shrubs (six feet in height at installation) such as Skyrocket Junipers or
Wichita Blue Junipers may also be substituted for evergreen trees in instances where
space is limited.
(p)
Detailed information on the landscape and irrigation plan submittal process, and inspection
and certification procedures to assess compliance with Sterling Ranch's water demand
management measures can be found in the Sterling Ranch Water Demand Management Initiatives.
See Section 9-76 .
(Rules of 8-26-2020(9), § 6.5; Res. No.
2022-08-02
, § 1, 8-26-2022; Res. No.
2023-04-02
, § 1, 4-19-2023)

documents.title: Sec. 5-152. - Additional requirements for icon and enhanced lots.
path: Sec. 5-152. - Additional requirements for icon and enhanced lots.
documents.text:
Icon and enhanced lots are defined as one-of-a-kind, highly visible, adjacent to community
features or amenities, and adjacent to high-traffic areas. The DRC reserves the right
to require additional landscape materials (plants, trees, screens, and/or berms) or
to restrict potentially unsightly elements such as sheds, trampolines, receptacles,
etc., from being highly visible on these lots. As examples, a highly visible lot near
the main entrance may be required to have additional plantings, whereas a lot adjacent
to a recreation area may have screening hedges to protect privacy. The DRC shall be
contacted to discuss submittal requirements. Refer to village-specific design guideline
booklets for icon lot determination for each respective village.
Enhanced Landscaping at Rear
(Rules of 8-26-2020(9), § 6.6)

documents.title: Sec. 5-153. - Example landscape plans.
documents.text:
The following example landscape plans are representative of landscape designs that
meet the landscape water budget of each associated lot size. The landscape water demand
for each lot will be calculated based on the selected irrigated water use zones (high,
moderate, and low). The Preapproved Plant List for Sterling Ranch, included as section 5-131 , organizes acceptable tree, shrub, grass and perennial species by their relative
irrigated water use zone and shall be used to classify selected plants into the appropriate
zone. Refer to section 5-131 .

documents.title: Sec. 5-177. - General intent and review compliance.
path: DIVISION 7. - DESIGN REVIEW PROCESS FOR BUILDERS
Sec. 5-177. - General intent and review compliance.
documents.text:
(a)
The Design Review Process is intended to manage and enforce the design standards contained
herein to achieve the maximum aesthetic benefits for the community and continue to
enhance property values. All submittals shall comply with the following procedural
requirements to ensure a timely process and in order to gain approval from the Design
Review Committee (DRC). The DRC shall strive to approve, approve with conditions,
or deny a complete set of Final and Concept Design Submittal documents within the
later to occur of 30 days after its receipt or ten days after the first meeting of
the DRC following its receipt. The DRC's failure to approve, approve with conditions
or deny a complete Approval Request within such period shall be deemed a denial of
such Approval Request.
(b)
It is required that the Owner retain assistance from a competent, licensed Architect.
Plans submitted for final DRC approval must be stamped by the Architect. The Builder
and their consultant should also carefully review the County's requirements, the Master
Declaration of Covenants, Conditions and Restrictions (CC&Rs), Rules and Regulations
regarding covenant enforcement as adopted by the CAB, as well as the Design Guidelines
prior to commencing the design review process.
(Rules of 8-26-2020(9), § 7(intro. ¶))

documents.title: Sec. 5-178. - Pre-design meeting.
path: DIVISION 7. - DESIGN REVIEW PROCESS FOR BUILDERS
documents.text:
Prior to preparing preliminary designs, it is required that the Builders and/or Builders'
representative meet with the DRC to discuss ideas of the design, concerns of the DRC
and site constraints of the neighborhood or individual site. These items will include
the following:
(1)
Approval of Design Team—Architect.
(2)
Garage configurations.
(3)
Proposed style of residence.
(4)
Douglas County requirements.
(5)
Easements, setbacks and drainage with adjacent site.
(6)
Enhanced or Icon Lots.
(7)
Percentage Requirements:
a.
Masonry.
b.
Front garages.
c.
Roof lines.
d.
Recessed balconies.
e.
Three-story masses.
(Rules of 8-26-2020(9), § 7.1)

documents.title: Sec. 5-179. - Concept design submittal.
path: DIVISION 7. - DESIGN REVIEW PROCESS FOR BUILDERS
documents.text:
Following the Pre-Design meeting, the Builders and/or Builders' licensed Architect
shall provide preliminary architectural design concepts for submittal to the DRC.
The submittal shall include two copies of the following in scaled, dated drawings
at minimum 24 inches by 36 inches in size:
(1)
A typical site plan, depicting how the homes will fit on a typical lot.
(2)
Floor plans, one-quarter inch per foot, including any accessory structures.
(3)
Front elevations at the same scale as floor plans.
(4)
Typical side and rear elevations.
(5)
Typical roof plans showing drainage with primary roof form identified. Refer to section 5-214 .
(6)
Color boards can be submitted if selections have been made at this time.
(7)
Floor plans and elevations illustrating how icon and enhanced lots will be addressed.
(Rules of 8-26-2020(9), § 7.2)

documents.title: Sec. 5-180. - Final design submittal.
path: DIVISION 7. - DESIGN REVIEW PROCESS FOR BUILDERS
documents.text:
Following Concept Design Submittal, the Builders and/or Builders' Architect shall
provide final stamped architectural and site plan suitable for construction for submittal
to the DRC. The submittal shall include two copies of the following in scaled, dated,
24-inch by 36-inch drawings:
(1)
A typical site plan, including final grading from a licensed civil engineer. The final
site plan shall include final proposed grade lines, top of finish floors including
walkouts, all site improvements, retaining walls, easements and setbacks.
(2)
Detailed floor and roof plans, one-quarter inch per foot, including any accessory
structures. All options shall be provided in addition to standard plans.
(3)
All front, rear, and side elevations shall be shown at the same scale as floor plans,
accurately depicting actual and proposed grading. Elevations shall also show maximum
roof height as calculated by Douglas County. All options shall be provided in addition
to standard elevations.
(4)
Wall, building sections and exterior details shall be provided.
(5)
All enhanced and icon lot elevations shall be provided.
(6)
Color and Material Palette books shall include a typed schedule of all paint, materials,
and specified finishes, scheme pages for each scheme showing physical paint samples,
and pictures of masonry, roof tile, and any other specified materials, renderings
of applied paint schemes to approved homes, and color application documents (trim-outs)
for each plan and all elevations.
(7)
Variances are discouraged; however, they may be considered on a case-by-case basis.
After preparing the final design plans, the Builders or Builders' representative shall
submit the final construction drawings to the DRC for approval. The DRC shall strive
to approve, approve with conditions, or deny a complete Final Approval Request within
the later to occur of 30 days after its receipt or ten days after the first meeting
of the DRC following its receipt. If the final plans are approved, the Builders and/or
Builders' representative may apply for the appropriate permits to begin construction.
(Rules of 8-26-2020(9), § 7.3)

documents.title: Sec. 5-181. - Landscape review.
path: DIVISION 7. - DESIGN REVIEW PROCESS FOR BUILDERS
documents.text:
As part of the Final Plan Submittal, the applicant shall submit a landscape and exterior
plan for review and approval. The submittal shall include the following in scaled,
dated, 24-inch by 36-inch drawings:
(1)
An expanded site plan of exterior materials. This shall include lot number and/or
address, including final grading from a licensed civil engineer. Final site plan shall
include final proposed grade lines, top of finish floors including walkouts, easements
and setbacks, all site improvements, retaining walls, screen walls, paving materials,
and installation details and notes.
(2)
A landscape plan identifying plant material locations and types. The landscape plan
shall include a plant legend keyed to the plan identifying plant species with size
and condition at planting. The plan shall include notes and details identifying soil
prep, mulch type and all products used for edging, weed fabric, etc.
(3)
A lighting plan identifying lighting locations, types, and schematic wiring and control.
The lighting plan shall include a schedule of products keyed to the lighting plan
identifying bulb type and wattage. All lighting is required to be Dark Sky compliant.
(4)
The applicant shall provide product submittals of all hardscape, landscape and lighting
materials to be used. These may be product cut sheets or physical samples.
(5)
Two or more plans may be combined as part of the same plan if legible.
(6)
The DRC is not responsible for reviewing or approving grading plans for any drainage
considerations. See Section 5-182 .
(Rules of 8-26-2020(9), § 7.4)

documents.title: Sec. 5-182. - General drainage.
path: DIVISION 7. - DESIGN REVIEW PROCESS FOR BUILDERS
documents.text:
(a)
Sterling Ranch Master Declaration of Covenants, Conditions and Restrictions requires
that there be no interference with the established drainage pattern on any property.
The established drainage pattern as engineered and constructed by the Builder prior
(or, in some cases, immediately following) conveyance or title from the Builder to
the individual homeowner.
(b)
Any Builder who changes the existing grading or drainages may void warranties applicable
to affected components of the home and shall be liable for all costs and expenses
of repairing such changes, or any costs, liabilities, damages or causes of action
arising out of such changes.
(c)
When installing landscaping, it is very important to ensure that water drains away
from the foundation of the house (but not onto neighboring properties) and that the
flow patterns prevent water from flowing under or against the house foundation, walkways,
sidewalks, and driveways into the street.
(d)
Landscaping should conform to the established drainage pattern.
(e)
Adverse effects to adjacent properties will not be tolerated.
(f)
The DRC is not responsible in any way for changes made to grading and/or drainage
while installing landscaping or other improvements. All County and State code requirements
are to be followed and are the sole responsibility of the homeowner. Any changes to
the drainage pattern that cause damage to any downstream party is totally and solely
the responsibility of the Builder who made the grade change or who permitted the grade
change to be made by a contractor, vendor, or other entity working on the property.
(g)
The DRC may require a report from a Colorado registered civil engineer with a P.E.
stamped plot plan and letter stating that drainage will not be changed in an adverse
way as part of landscaping or improvement plan approval for plans, including, but
not limited to:
(1)
Patios.
(2)
Covered Decks.
(3)
Sport Courts.
(4)
Raised or bermed planting beds.
(Rules of 8-26-2020(9), § 7.5)

documents.title: Sec. 5-185. - Non-liability disclaimer.
path: DIVISION 7. - DESIGN REVIEW PROCESS FOR BUILDERS
documents.text:
(a)
These Design Guidelines supplement the Douglas County building and Sterling Ranch
Development zoning codes. The Design Guidelines do not supersede any existing applicable
codes or ordinances. Neither the Master Developer, the Design Review Committee (DRC),
nor the Community Authority Board (CAB) assume responsibility for plan review of,
or conformance to, applicable local codes or ordinances. The DRC's purpose in plan
review is to meet the intent of the Design Guidelines and supporting documents in
keeping with the overall vision of the Sterling Ranch community.
(b)
Neither the DRC or the CAB, any member thereof, nor the Master Developer shall be
liable to any Builder/owner or other person for any loss or damage claimed on account
of any of the following:
(1)
The approval or disapproval of any plans, drawings and specifications, whether or
not defective.
(2)
The construction or performance of any work, whether or not pursuant to approved plans,
drawings and specifications regardless of any inspections by the DRC during the course
of construction.
(c)
Every Builder or other person by submission of plans and specifications to the DRC
for approval agrees that he will not bring any action or suit against the DRC, any
of its members, nor the Master Developer, or the CAB regarding any action taken by
the DRC.
(d)
Approval from the DRC of any improvements at Sterling Ranch only refers to the Sterling
Ranch Guidelines and in no way implies conformance with local government regulations.
It will be the sole responsibility of the Builder/owner to comply with all applicable
government ordinances or regulations, including but not limited to zoning ordinances
and local building codes.
(e)
Contact info. For questions contact:
Sterling Ranch DRC
submit@sterlingranchdrc.com
(Rules of 8-26-2020(9), § 7.8)

documents.title: Sec. 5-212. - Utilities and conservation.
documents.text:
(a)
Solution overview.
(1)
Sustainability and conservation is important to the Sterling Ranch home buyer and
central to the community.
(2)
The CAB has partnered with Siemens to offer a leading-edge solution for utility monitoring,
sustainability, and conservation.
(3)
This solution will help homeowners save money on their utility bills while conserving
the beautiful nature of Sterling Ranch.
(b)
Solution description; water metering and conservation.
(1)
Homes in Sterling Ranch will have separate water meters for indoor and outdoor water
usage.
a.
This allows the Community Authority Board to bill separate rates for indoor and outdoor
water usage.
b.
These separate rates more accurately reflect system costs and are important to incentivize
conservation of outdoor water usage.
c.
The water meters used in Sterling Ranch will also enable feedback to homeowners regarding
water usage and enable homeowners to remotely shut off their water in case of a leak.
(2)
Homes in Sterling Ranch will also utilize a smart irrigation controller.
a.
The smart irrigation controller automatically adjusts watering schedules based on
real-time weather data;
b.
This will allow homeowners to conserve water and save money without additional effort.
(c)
Real-time utility feedback and smart home integration.
(1)
Homes in Sterling Ranch will utilize cutting edge utility monitoring technology to
provide homeowners with feedback about their utility usage.
a.
Two utility monitoring devices will be used to collect real-time utility information
for gas, water, and electric;
b.
Homeowners will have the ability to access their data and view usage patterns;
c.
This will allow homeowners in Sterling Ranch to adjust their usage over time to save
money and conserve resources.
(2)
Utility data will also be connected with the home automation system.
a.
This allows homeowners to view utility usage directly in their home automation app,
create notifications and usage alerts, and automate certain functions in their home
based on utility data;
b.
This will also enable future updates to the home automation software that will help
homeowners conserve even more with less effort.
(d)
Logistics and support. Utility and conservation components will be available through technology packages
offered by Siemens.
(1)
Packages are broken out by trade (plumbing, landscaper, etc.).
(2)
Builder subcontractors will purchase and install the package corresponding with their
trade.
(3)
Siemens will be responsible for activating the smart irrigation controller and utility
monitoring devices after installation.
(4)

documents.title: Sec. 5-212. - Utilities and conservation.
documents.text:
Landscapers will be responsible for programming watering schedules for the smart irrigation
controller.
(5)
Trade-specific technology packages are further detailed in division 9 of this article.
(Rules of 8-26-2020(9), § 9.4, app. B)

documents.title: Sec. 5-213. - Solar and electric vehicle readiness.
path: Sec. 5-213. - Solar and electric vehicle readiness.
documents.text:
(a)
Solution overview.
(1)
Demand for solar panels and electric vehicle chargers continues to increase.
(2)
In many communities, the need to tear out drywall to install these systems is a significant
barrier to adoption.
(3)
As a truly 21st century community, every home in Sterling Ranch will be equipped with
pre-wire for solar panels and electric vehicle chargers.
(4)
This will allow homeowners to easily install these systems if they desire while increasing
the resale value of the home even if they do not.
(b)
Solution description.
(1)
Solar pre-wire. Homes must have conduit placed from the roof to the electric load center.
(2)
Solar Made Simple program.
a.
The offering of the Solar Made Simple program, through which the builder provides
homeowners the option to have zero down payment residential solar installed on the
home is required. As part of the Solar Made Simple program, an opt-out form will be
required and is available from CAB. If no opt-out form is provided the builder shall
make a zero down payment power purchase agreement (PPA) or zero down payment lease
option for residential solar available to homeowners.
b.
Builders will work with CAB approved providers; please contact CAB for additional
details.
(3)
Electric vehicle pre-wire.
a.
Homes must have a NEMA 14-50 outlet in the garage to enable installation of an electric
vehicle charging station.
b.
Each builder shall offer a battery storage option for each home.
(c)
Logistics.
(1)
Builders will be responsible for installation of conduit and outlets in order to meet
the requirements outlined in this section.
(2)
The Community Authority Board reserves the right to inspect homes for these conduit
runs and outlets and enforce their placement.
(3)
If a home is found to be out of compliance, the builder will be responsible for all
costs associated with bringing the home into compliance.
(4)
Because of this, builders are strongly encouraged to make sure conduit and outlets
are placed before drywall has been hung.
(Rules of 8-26-2020(9), § 9.4, app. D; Res. No.
2023-07-01
, § 1, 7-19-2023)

documents.title: Sec. 5-214. - Conclusion.
documents.text:
(a)
The inherent characteristics of Sterling Ranch reach beyond the duty of conserving
its natural surroundings. By following the design principles outlined in this article,
the built environment of Sterling Ranch works in concert to protect and promote an
enduring affinity to this master-planned, intelligently designed community. Smartly
integrating technology into multiple aspects of the community and strategically offering
residents an ability to contour their homes to the nature of their day.
(b)
Sterling Ranch is a carefully crafted place, and a home that residents will foster,
enjoy and express with gratitude for generations to come. You are now part of the
enduring character of this one-of-a-kind community. Welcome to The Nature of Sterling
Ranch.
(Rules of 8-26-2020(9), § 8)

documents.title: Sec. 5-249. - Process overview.
documents.text:
(a)
Ordering process.
(1)
Technology solutions must be ordered through Siemens on behalf of the Sterling Ranch
Community Authority Board (CAB).
(2)
When ready to order, the home builder/sub-contractor must purchase the required kit
for Sterling Ranch at (https://sterlingranchorders.com/customer/account/login).
(3)
Home builder/sub-contractor must provide a purchase order at the time of ordering
showing the home address for each kit being ordered.
(4)
Accurate order lead times will be provided shortly after the order has been placed.
(5)
Estimated lead times can be between three to six weeks and may vary depending on quantities
and technology packages being ordered.
(6)
Invoicing will be provided at the time of the order.
(7)
Packages will be available for pickup at the specified Siemens warehouse, or optional
service, delivered to a Siemens certified installer chosen by the home builder.
(b)
Installation overview.
(1)
Home builder responsibilities are to purchase technology packages from Siemens as
required by the design guidelines for:
a.
Low voltage.
b.
Line voltage.
c.
Plumbing.
d.
Landscape.
e.
HVAC.
(2)
Home builders are encouraged to schedule an appointment with their subcontractors
and Siemens so that subcontractors are informed of the installation methodologies.
(3)
Home builders and their installers should follow the wiring specifications that are
shown in sections 5-250 through 5-257 .
(4)
Site supervisors must complete the Siemens pre-commissioning installation checklist
to ensure all packages are installed properly at least two weeks prior to home closing.
(c)
Commissioning overview.
(1)
Home builder responsibilities:
a.
Home builders must provide Siemens and any other companies critical to the technology
installation and commissioning process with updated build and closing schedules.
b.
Home builders must install the equipment as depicted in sections 5-250 through 5-257 at least two weeks prior to scheduled closing.
1.
Home builders are recommended to have their subcontractors complete installation four
weeks prior to home close.
2.
This leaves time for site supervisors to check for proper installation and fix any
issues prior to the installation deadline two weeks before closing.
(2)
If Siemens attempts their commissioning and installation is not completed properly,
Siemens will distribute a report with all known issues.
(3)
Home builders will be required to complete any necessary repairs at least one week
prior to home closing and notify Siemens following completion.
(4)

documents.title: Sec. 5-249. - Process overview.
documents.text:
Trip charges will be assessed for builders who repeatedly require notification of

(5)
Please reach out to Siemens to train your subcontractors on installation and avoid

documents.title: Sec. 5-258. - Home technology solutions and requirements.
path: Sec. 5-258. - Home technology solutions and requirements.
documents.text:
(a)
Overview.
(1)
This section and sections 5-212 , 5-213 and 5-259 —5-261 outlines requirements for key home technology solutions in Sterling Ranch.
(2)
These solutions will help Sterling Ranch develop a core identity that resonates with
residents while helping the CAB achieve its conservation, connectivity, and safety
objectives.
(3)
The solutions in this section are intended to help builder teams understand and articulate
the value these key solutions provide for residents.
(4)
Additional resources and training are available to the builder team to help them understand
and articulate the value proposition of these solutions.
(5)
Labeling in this section and sections 5-212 , 5-213 and 5-259 —5-261 will not match one to one with the execution guides outlined in section division 9 of this article.
(b)
Value proposition.
(1)
The key solutions outlined in this section and sections 5-212 , 5-213 and 5-259 —5-261 will help differentiate homes in Sterling Ranch from surrounding communities.
(2)
We expect these solutions to add up to $5,000.00 in cost, but add far more significant
value to the sales price.
(3)
Builders who effectively educate their teams on these solutions will drive significant
value for their home buyers.
(4)
Resources are available to help builder teams maximize the value of these solutions.
(Rules of 8-26-2020(9), § 9.4)

documents.title: Sec. 5-259. - Home automation.
documents.text:
(a)
Solution overview.
(1)
Home automation has become an expectation for new home buyers and serves to assist
the CAB in achieving its safety, connectivity, and conservation objectives.
(2)
The CAB has partnered with Siemens to offer a leading-edge solution to whole-home
automation.
(3)
This solution combines a wide array of functionalities into one intuitive app that
will continue to evolve over time.
(4)
This section and sections 5-212 , 5-213 , 5-258 , 5-260 and 5-261 lay out a minimum standard for home analytics, conservation, and automation in Sterling
Ranch.
(5)
Home builders are encouraged to add additional compatible devices to their base home
to maximize their value proposition.
(b)
Solution description. Home analytics automation requirements in Sterling Ranch include:
(1)
Home Automation Hub;
(2)
Home Automation Tablet;
(3)
Thermostat Control;
(4)
Lighting Control (Five Zones);
(5)
Mobile App Based Security System Control;
(6)
Smart Irrigation System Control;
(7)
Water Shutoff Valve Control;
(8)
Real Time Utility Data and Analytics;
(9)
Notification of Community Events and Announcements;
(10)
Wireless mesh networking system.
(c)
Logistics and support. Home automation components will be purchased through technology packages offered
by Siemens.
(1)
Packages are broken out by trade (low voltage, line voltage, HVAC, etc.).
(2)
Builder subcontractors will purchase and install the package corresponding with their
trade.
(3)
Siemens will be responsible for activating the home automation package components
after subcontractor installation is complete.
(4)
Trade-specific technology packages are further detailed in this division.
(d)
Suggested additions.
(1)
Suggested additions to base homes include:
a.
Connected door lock.
b.
Connected garage door opener.
c.
Connected doorbell camera.
d.
Additional zones of lighting.
e.
IP camera pre-wire.
(2)
Suggested homeowner options include:
a.
Shade control.
b.
Audio/visual control.
c.
IP cameras and additional security devices.
d.
Connected flood sensors.
e.
Connected smoke and carbon monoxide detectors.
(Rules of 8-26-2020(9), § 9.4, app. A)

documents.title: Sec. 5-260. - Internet and networking.
documents.text:
(a)
Solution overview.
(1)
Great Internet is a differentiator in Sterling Ranch and is critical for harnessing
the full power of the home analytics and automation systems.
(2)
Fiber Internet, proper cabling, and wireless mesh systems enable high-quality connectivity.
(b)
Solution description.
(1)
In-home wireless mesh network.
a.
Every home in Sterling Ranch is equipped with a best-in-class wireless mesh networking
system.
b.
Wireless mesh networking systems are state-of-the-art technology, designed to provide
the best Wi-Fi experience available.
c.
This solution will provide great whole-home Wi-Fi coverage for the vast majority of
homeowners, but, if needed, homeowners can easily add additional auxiliary access
points to their mesh system after move-in.
(2)
In-home cabling.
a.
Homes in Sterling Ranch have CAT 6 cables to enable hard-wired connections.
b.
Each home shall have a minimum of three CAT 6 drops and one Coaxial drop.
c.
One CAT 6 drop must be to a central location on the main floor where a wireless access
point can be installed to enable the home's wireless network.
d.
One CAT 6 and one Coaxial drop must be to an entertainment location within the home.
(c)
Logistics.
(1)
Fiber Internet installation from back of lot to the home is a builder responsibility.
a.
The builder is responsible for paying for fiber Internet installation from the back
of the lot to the home.
b.
This process includes running microduct from the back of the lot to the home, mounting
a fiber box on the side of the home, pulling fiber, and installing an ONT.
c.
Sections 5-250 and 5-257 provide additional details including recommended contractors, method, and approach.
(2)
Wireless mesh networking devices and activation will be available through technology
packages offered by Siemens.
a.
Siemens will install and activate mesh networking devices during final commissioning.
b.
Trade-specific technology packages are further detailed in this division.
(3)
Cabling will be performed by a low voltage provider and is not included in the technology
packages offered by Siemens.
(4)
Home builders will work with a fiber Internet installer in order to arrange installation
of fiber to the home.
(Rules of 8-26-2020(9), § 9.4, app. C)

documents.title: Sec. 5-283. - Vision.
documents.article: ARTICLE III. - ASCENT VILLAGE DESIGN PRINCIPLES
path: ARTICLE III. - ASCENT VILLAGE DESIGN PRINCIPLES
documents.text:
Ascent Village is where every walk of life begins. Rising up in the master plan of
Sterling Ranch with beautiful views of the Highlands Ranch open space to the east
and the mountains to the west, Ascent Village offers the first Village Center in Sterling
Ranch. Surrounded by the wildlife Colorado has to offer, Ascent Village is a collection
of characteristic neighborhoods defined by location and distinctive architectural
styles. Ascent Village's architectural styles are rooted in Colorado vernaculars and
will distinguish Ascent Village's character with a unique sense of place.
(Rules of 8-26-2020(10), § 1.1)

documents.title: Sec. 5-284. - Site description.
documents.article: ARTICLE III. - ASCENT VILLAGE DESIGN PRINCIPLES
path: ARTICLE III. - ASCENT VILLAGE DESIGN PRINCIPLES
documents.text:
Situated in the middle of Sterling Ranch, Ascent Village continues the thoughtful
design, environmentally conscious and resident-centric vision that is Sterling Ranch.
Centered within Ascent Village is Sterling Ranch's first mixed-use village center.
Bordered to the west by Burns Park and interspersed with a regional trail and wildlife
corridor, residents experience Colorado's wildlife and natural landscape. To the east
is planned an age-restricted community appealing to the more mature buyer complete
with enhanced amenities, trail systems and gathering places geared toward the active
adult.
(Rules of 8-26-2020(10), § 1.2)

documents.title: Sec. 5-331. - Architectural approach.
documents.article: ARTICLE III. - ASCENT VILLAGE DESIGN PRINCIPLES
path: ARTICLE III. - ASCENT VILLAGE DESIGN PRINCIPLES
documents.text:
(a)
Recalling Colorado's historic park neighborhoods that edge its cities and the sprawling
prairie lands just beyond, Ascent Village echoes the charming sophistication of early
Denver and its neighboring suburbs with a refined, modern touch.
(b)
Inspired by the sprawling character of its terrain, Ascent Village will feature a
series of architectural styles: Colorado Cottage, Colorado Farmhouse, Mid-Century
Ranch, High Country Ranch, and Modern Prairie.
Architectural Styles
(c)
Organic and simple in their structures, Colorado Cottage, Colorado Farmhouse, and
High Country Ranch introduce a palette of agrarian vernaculars to Sterling Ranch that
are inherently Colorado. Alternatively, Mid-Century Ranch and Modern Prairie represent
the Modern Colorado aesthetics for the village. Spirited and structured, these vernaculars
will provide additional language to aid the ever-evolving aesthetic toward more polished
executions.
(d)
To further distinguish Ascent Village, the village will feature active adult product
that will be limited to the village's Colorado Agrarian vernaculars: Colorado Cottage,
Colorado Farmhouse, and High Country Ranch. While the rest of the village will be
comprised of all five styles, Mid-Century Ranch will be limited to single-story ranch
homes to maintain the style's authenticity.
(e)
Through its unique array of style characters, Ascent Village will further develop
the essential vision of Sterling Ranch, embellished with a fresh approach that grows
and evolves into a definitive aesthetic for the village that will enhance the overall
community.
(Rules of 8-26-2020(10), § 4.1)

documents.title: Sec. 5-332. - Village architecture overview.
documents.article: ARTICLE III. - ASCENT VILLAGE DESIGN PRINCIPLES
path: ARTICLE III. - ASCENT VILLAGE DESIGN PRINCIPLES
documents.text:
(a)
Colorado cottage. A reflection of Colorado's agrarian homesteads, Colorado Cottage is alluring in its
simplicity. articulated by subtle stone textures, and clean detailing.
Colorado Cottage
(b)
Colorado farmhouse. Drawing from the rural farmhouse vernacular that is widespread throughout eastern
Colorado, Colorado Farmhouse is a fresh take on this classic style. Large porches
and playful colors mark this distinct style.
Colorado Farmhouse
(c)
High country ranch. The High Country Ranch style is a careful contiguity between rustic and contemporary
that gives more of a modern mountain lodge feel. Large masses of stone and wood enhance
the additive nature of this style, topping it with a metal roof.
High Country Ranch
(d)
Modern prairie. Structured and sophisticated, the Modern Prairie is better known for its horizontal
expression of its roof forms, and is composed of bold forms, rich materials, and clean,
sturdy details.
Modern Prairie
(Rules of 8-26-2020(10), § 4.2(intro. ¶))

documents.title: Sec. 5-333. - Colorado cottage.
documents.article: ARTICLE III. - ASCENT VILLAGE DESIGN PRINCIPLES
path: ARTICLE III. - ASCENT VILLAGE DESIGN PRINCIPLES
documents.text:
(a)
Generally. Capturing the quaint charm of Colorado's early homestead structures, as found in
areas such as Wash Park, the Colorado Cottage is characterized by its beautiful simplicity.
Reflecting traditional folk house construction, the style follows rectilinear plan
formats with simple massing. Roofs echo the modest, welcoming form with front-facing
gables, sheds, hips, and dormer roofs. Adding to its appeal, the style features a
warm material palette. Comprised predominately of board and batten with siding accents
of horizontal clapboard or shingle, rugged stone, and clean detailing, the materials
further imbue the style with an organic grace. Inviting and alluring, the Colorado
Cottage is equally elegant and humble, establishing a charmingly new aesthetic for
Ascent Village.
Cottage Aesthetic Character
(b)
Style description. Organic and simple, the Colorado Cottage is composed primarily of board and batten
with accents of horizontal cladding or shingle siding. The combination of rough stone
textures, structured window compositions, and simplistic detailing furthers the juxtaposition
of natural and refined elements that is characteristic of the style. At roofs, both
composition shingle and concrete roof tile are allowed. The color palette contributes
to the style's modest allure with light tonal hues and complementary yet neutral accents
that emphasize the transition of textures versus individual elements. Overall, there
is a sense of peaceful balance both in the material palette and in its application.
Colorado Cottage Illustration
(c)
Style details.
(1)
Massing.
a.
Emphasis on one story is preferred, two story limited.
b.
Primary roof form is broken into segments with intersecting gable and shed dormers.
c.
Simple, yet elegant massing is preferred.
(2)
Roof forms.
a.
Low roof pitches are preferred.
b.
Gable, hip, shed, and bonnet roof forms are allowed.
c.
Careful compositions that avoid overly complex and confusing roof combinations are
desired.
d.
A clear hierarchy of forms is required.
(3)
Windows and doors.
a.
Ribbons of windows well placed.
b.
Classic window mullions to enhance character.
c.
Bay Windows added to express window groupings.
d.
Shutters should be avoided.
(4)
Materials.
a.
Single siding, vertical board and batten siding, or horizontal clapboard, or any combination
thereof may be employed, with less emphasis on horizontal clapboard.
b.
Variation of siding types may be used for color blocking and creative application
of color schemes.
c.
Metal, composition shingles, and concrete tile are acceptable roof materials. Metal

documents.title: Sec. 5-333. - Colorado cottage.
documents.article: ARTICLE III. - ASCENT VILLAGE DESIGN PRINCIPLES
path: ARTICLE III. - ASCENT VILLAGE DESIGN PRINCIPLES
documents.text:
must be clean in its appearance.
(5)
Enhanced elements. Exposed wood posts, beams, corbels, and rafter tails are preferred and contribute
to the refined, rustic beauty of this style.
(Rules of 8-26-2020(10), § 4.2(A))

documents.title: Sec. 5-334. - Colorado farmhouse.
documents.article: ARTICLE III. - ASCENT VILLAGE DESIGN PRINCIPLES
path: ARTICLE III. - ASCENT VILLAGE DESIGN PRINCIPLES
documents.text:
(a)
Generally. Rooted in the tradition of the farmhouse vernacular that is widespread throughout
Colorado's abundant farmland, brought by farmers and ranchers, the Colorado Farmhouse
is a fresh take on this classic style. Simplistic and understated in its forms, the
vernacular features clean details. The material palette is expressed through clapboard
and vertical board and batten siding, standing seam metal roof accents, and light,
playful colors contrasted by bold accents. Firmly celebrating Colorado's agrarian
roots, the Colorado Farmhouse captures the charming simplicity of the style with a
touch of refined sophistication.
Farmhouse Aesthetic Character
(b)
Style description. Capturing the charm and simplicity of classic farmhouse vernaculars, Colorado Farmhouse
style is both playful and clean in its expression. The facade's simplistic form is
further articulated with a mixture of clapboard, vertical, and board and batten siding
types. Though not essential to the style, stone and brick may be incorporated to add
texture and movement in small amounts. All in all, the materials support the pure
simplicity of the style.
Colorado Farmhouse Illustration
(c)
Style details.
(1)
Massing.
a.
Two-Story massing broken by front porches.
b.
Simple, yet elegant massing is preferred.
c.
Wrap-around porches are encouraged.
(2)
Roof forms.
a.
A mixture of steep and low roof pitches are preferred.
b.
Gable, hip, shed, and bonnet roof forms are allowed.
c.
Careful compositions that avoid overly complex and confusing roof combinations are
desired.
d.
A clear hierarchy of forms is required.
(3)
Windows and doors.
a.
Logic in the placement of windows is required.
b.
Window shutters are allowed.
c.
Large glass expanses, and structured fenestration compositions are encouraged for
this style.
d.
Windows with or without mullions may be incorporated; without is encouraged.
(4)
Materials.
a.
Clapboard or vertical board and batten siding, or a combination of the two siding
types, may be employed.
b.
Variation of siding types is allowable for color blocking and creative application
of color schemes on a case-by-case basis.
c.
Metal, composition shingles, and concrete tile are acceptable roof materials. Metal
must be clean in its appearance.
d.
Brick and stone are allowed, though not required for this style.
(5)
Enhanced elements.
a.
Clean and simple detailing, wood posts, and beams are preferred and contribute to
a feeling of refined simplicity.
b.
Brackets at porches are not encouraged.
c.
Playful colors are contrasted by bold accents.
(Rules of 8-26-2020(10), § 4.2(B))

documents.title: Sec. 5-335. - Mid-century ranch.
documents.article: ARTICLE III. - ASCENT VILLAGE DESIGN PRINCIPLES
path: ARTICLE III. - ASCENT VILLAGE DESIGN PRINCIPLES
documents.text:
(a)
Generally. Scattered throughout Colorado's neighborhoods, the Mid-Century Ranch style is iconic
in nature, expressed with angular, simplistic forms and playful details. Drawing from
this heritage, the Mid-Century Ranch refines the notable style with cleaner lines
and textures, while maintaining its spirited essence. Strong, sculptural gable roof
lines frame a simple form, which is further articulated by large glass expanses, stone
accents, and siding. Its material palette is expressed in fresh masonry textures,
and clean cladding while the color palette reinforces the purity of the style's forms.
Mid-Century Ranch Aesthetic Character
(b)
Style description. Pure and iconic in form, the Mid-Century Ranch is further distinguished by its fresh
material palette and playful employ of color. Comprised primarily of a variety of
siding types, the form is expressed through a mixture of horizontal and vertical clapboard,
with stone elements, and clean, strong details. The variety of siding types allows
for creative color applications, adding to the cheerful nature of the style. Stone
can range from rubble profiles to clean and linear stacked-bond blocks and squares;
brick may also be employed. Additionally, wood tile may be incorporated, though it
is not essential to execution of this style. Ultimately, the materials, whether inspired
by historic applications or contemporary profiles, enhance the overall appeal of this
spirited style.
Mid-Century Modern Illustration
(c)
Style details.
(1)
Massing.
a.
Typically, asymmetrical with strong gable forms.
b.
Two-story applications of this style shall not be permitted.
(2)
Roof forms.
a.
Simple and strong gable forms (front gable, or back-to-front) are the dominant roof
forms.
b.
Flying shed roofs are not permitted; structured and simple compositions are encouraged.
c.
Asymmetrical gable roof forms.
(3)
Windows and doors.
a.
Large glass expanses and atypical fenestration compositions are encouraged.
b.
Vaulted ceilings and interiors with floor-to-ceiling glass are encouraged.
(4)
Materials.
a.
Natural materials help give the modern forms a Colorado feel.
b.
Stone, brick, and wood tile are all allowable materials; stone can range from rubble
to clean stacked-bond block profiles.
c.
Composition shingles or concrete tile are all acceptable roof materials.
(5)
Enhanced elements.
a.
Vertical elements that accent the strong horizontal massing add texture to forms.
b.
Playful use of materials will enhance the overall look.
c.
Post and beam construction at enhanced elements.
(Rules of 8-26-2020(10), § 4.2(C))

documents.title: Sec. 5-336. - High country ranch.
documents.article: ARTICLE III. - ASCENT VILLAGE DESIGN PRINCIPLES
path: ARTICLE III. - ASCENT VILLAGE DESIGN PRINCIPLES
documents.text:
(a)
Generally. Drawing inspiration from both mountain and prairie influences, the High Country Ranch
style employs sturdy timber detailing with a sprawling ranch form and simple massing.
Resembling early homesteads, the form is asymmetrical, accentuated by an array of
materials, consistent with the developed-over-time character of this style. While
inspired by earlier forms, the High Country Ranch style is more controlled in its
execution than past iterations. A mixture of gable-dominated roof forms break up the
horizontal form, while strong fenestration compositions and stone elements further
solidify the structure. Its modern material palette brings a sense of sophistication
to the aesthetic, establishing a style for Ascent Village that is both rustic and
refined.
High Country Ranch Aesthetic Character
(b)
Style description. The material palette consists primarily of warm wood or cementitious siding, with
wood detailing and stone elements. Composition shingle or concrete roof tile combines
with clean modern metal roof accents, which further reinforces the ranch aesthetic.
Typically, the stone resembles large limestone profiles; however, the profile can
range from rough, over-grouted applications to modern block and dry-stacked ledge
treatments. Overall, the form reflects the style's inspired homestead aesthetic, while
its materials contrast, offering a refined beauty to the rustic nature of the style.
High Country Ranch Illustration
(c)
Style details.
(1)
Massing.
a.
Simple massing with cross gables. Nested gables are encouraged.
b.
Stone as dominant masses.
c.
Simple forms broken by large entry porches.
(2)
Roof forms.
a.
Gable, hip, and bonnet roofs are all components of this style.
b.
A mix of roof pitches provides a built-over-time feel.
c.
Steeple roof slopes for main roof.
(3)
Windows and doors.
a.
Windows with a vertical emphasis and employed in ribbons or pairs are encouraged.
b.
Windows without mullions may be incorporated.
c.
Clustered windows are preferred with large glass expanses at enhanced areas.
(4)
Materials.
a.
Wood siding, cementitious siding, and stone are the primary materials. The mixture
of materials reinforces this style's built-over-time character.
b.
Standing seam metal, composition shingles, or concrete tile are all acceptable roof
materials.
c.
Material and paint colors to achieve a warmer feel with natural beauty.
(5)
Enhanced elements. Oversized wood posts, beams, and wide trim elements support this style and should
be strong, sturdy, and clean in their execution.
(Rules of 8-26-2020(10), § 4.2(D))

documents.title: Sec. 5-337. - Modern prairie.
documents.article: ARTICLE III. - ASCENT VILLAGE DESIGN PRINCIPLES
path: ARTICLE III. - ASCENT VILLAGE DESIGN PRINCIPLES
documents.text:
(a)
Generally. Staying true to the spirit of Prairie architecture, the Modern Prairie style reflects
the rolling hills and ravines of its terrain. Deriving its form from the land, the
Modern Prairie style is horizontal by nature and is expressed through clean lines
and solid massing. Roof lines layer and jut out in exaggerated overhangs, amassed
over large glass expanses that bring the outdoors in. Glass and masonry hug the earth,
grounding the solidity of form and line expressed in the style. Overall, the strength
of the style merges with a bold material palette offering an aesthetic that is quintessentially
Colorado.
Modern Prairie Aesthetic Character
(b)
Style description. Horizontal in nature, the Modern Prairie style is expressed with generous roof overhangs,
large glass expanses, and a layering of roof forms, producing a style that is boldly
sophisticated. The overall massing is structured and simple, while ribbons of windows
emphasize the well-composed form. Carefully crafted trim and panel detailing may be
added, but in more modern applications, as a nod to the style's early Arts and Crafts
roots. An artful material palette comprised of varying siding types and clean masonry
veneers anchors the style, contributing a sense of strength and beauty to the ordered
form.
Modern Prairie Illustration
(c)
Style details.
(1)
Massing.
a.
Simple, structured vertical massing with strong horizontal roof lines.
b.
Well balanced massing, either in a symmetrical or asymmetrical form, is essential
to the execution of this style.
(2)
Roof forms.
a.
Low-pitched roof, hip roofs are typical; gable roofs are also appropriate.
b.
Large, roof overhangs accentuate the style's horizontal lines.
c.
Lot pitch roofs are encouraged.
(3)
Windows and doors.
a.
Clean, window trim and panel detailing, as pertaining to the style.
b.
Carefully composed window compositions, often appearing in rows, or ribbons.
(4)
Materials.
a.
Stone, brick, and a variety of siding types are all allowable materials.
b.
Masonry shall be clean in both its appearance and application.
c.
Composition shingles, or concrete tile are acceptable roof materials.
(5)
Enhanced elements.
a.
Additional panel trim detailing, wrapping corner windows, is encouraged.
b.
Elements should be solid and bold in appearance, yet clean in their expression.
(Rules of 8-26-2020(10), § 4.2)

documents.title: Sec. 5-353. - Ascent Village landscaping standards.
documents.article: ARTICLE III. - ASCENT VILLAGE DESIGN PRINCIPLES
path: ARTICLE III. - ASCENT VILLAGE DESIGN PRINCIPLES
documents.text:
The following design principles provide a framework for successful implementation
of the desired conservation landscape characteristics of Ascent Village:
(1)
Turf grass should be used selectively within the front yard landscape composition.
Avoid creating nonfunctional and difficult-to-irrigate turf areas less than eight
feet in width (tree lawns or subsurface irrigated areas excluded).
(2)
While native, naturalized or adapted plant species commonly found in the region are
desired, these plant materials may be organized in informal groupings and massings,
or they may be organized in a more formal or structured manner that responds to forms
in the architecture or hardscape.
(3)
Design for a low-water, low-maintenance approach. Plant material that will spread
and naturalize requiring water on an as-needed basis is encouraged.
(4)
A mixture of deciduous and evergreen plant material should be selected to ensure seasonal
interest. Composition of plant size, leaf texture, and bloom color should be considered
to provide visual diversity.
(5)
Utilize side yards in front of wing fences to expand the front yard composition and
screen unusable side yard areas from view. Planting design should complement the architecture.
Site furnishings such as trellises, arbors and planters that play off the architecture
are encouraged as well.
(6)
Plants should be grouped into hydrozones (areas of similar water needs).
(7)
Consider drainage patterns, solar orientation, and exposure.
(8)
Vertical layering is encouraged. Canopy trees provide spatial structure and the framework
for smaller tree and shrub planting. Groupings of native and ornamental grasses, shrubs,
and perennials provide eye-level elements and visual interest that link the architecture
to ground-level elements such as groundcover plants, specialty paving, and potted
plants.
(9)
Plant material should be massed to define outdoor spaces, enhance the streetscape,
respect the architecture, and reinforce the primary entry.
(10)
Massing of species is recommended to provide strong swaths of texture, color, contrast
and visual interest throughout the community.
(Rules of 8-26-2020(10), § 5.1)

documents.title: Sec. 5-354. - Ascent Village preferred character plantings.

(a)
General character of landscape area. While the landscape character of Ascent Village supports the ideals of a conservation
landscape, plant material should be arranged in massings capitalizing on vertical
layering and be planted in a denser arrangement than one might see elsewhere in Sterling
Ranch. Smaller, multi-stem trees and spreading groundcovers and perennials should
be taken advantage of to fill landscape areas on residential lots.
(b)
Tree and plant materials approved lists. An approved list of tree and plant materials has been established for the Sterling
Ranch community. The following trees and plants are a few that are encouraged and
